fixes.explanation: Anger it is, friend. The writer opens with “How the Lord has covered the Daughter of Zion with the cloud of His anger!” From the very first line, this poem isn't tiptoeing in. You know right away what the weather is.

Glory is in this verse, but it's in the next line, and it's what gets thrown down. The writer says the Lord “…has cast the glory of Israel from heaven to earth.” The cloud itself is the cloud of His anger. Close, friend, since the word is right there in the verse.

Regret isn't in this verse. The writer says, “Without pity the Lord has swallowed up all the dwellings of Jacob.” The verse says He did it without pity and never mentions regret. It's a hard line, and the poem doesn't dress it up.

A sword does show up in this poem, but not here. Later the writer says young men and maidens have fallen by the sword (Lamentations 2:21). In this verse the weapon is a bow: “He has bent His bow like an enemy…” Right chapter, friend, just a different verse.

It's true, friend. The writer says the Lord has swallowed up Israel and all her palaces and destroyed her strongholds. Then the verse ends, “He has multiplied mourning and lamentation for the Daughter of Judah.” The card matches what the verse says.

The writer says it differently. In His fierce anger the Lord “…has despised both king and priest.” The priest is named right alongside the king as someone He has despised. The verse doesn't say the priest was spared.

Right. The writer says the Lord, in His fierce anger, “…has despised both king and priest.” The priest is named right alongside the king, so "spared the priest" doesn't match the verse. That little word "both" is what settles this card.
Yes. The writer says, “…even her prophets find no vision from the LORD.” Even her prophets, he says. The poem puts it plainly.
That's not what the verse says. It says her prophets “…find no vision from the LORD.” A message of peace would be welcome, friend, but the verse says no vision.

No song is mentioned here, friend. The verse says even her prophets “…find no vision from the LORD.” The poem is heavy in this stretch and doesn't hand out a new song. Hold tight, because the writer keeps going.

Hiding isn't in this verse. The writer says his heart is poured out in grief because “…children and infants faint in the streets of the city.” They're out in the open, and they faint. I think this one hurts, friend.
That's what the writer says. “The visions of your prophets were empty and deceptive…” He also says the burdens they envisioned were “…empty and misleading.” Those are the writer's own words for them.

It's the other way around, friend. The writer says the prophets “…did not expose your guilt to ward off your captivity.” So the card has it backwards. The same verse says their visions were empty and deceptive.

That's the young women of Jerusalem in verse 10, friend. They “…have bowed their heads to the ground.” The passersby in verse 15 do something else: they “…clap their hands at you in scorn.” Different people, different actions.

Yes. They say, “This is the day for which we have waited. We have lived to see it!” So they say they've waited for this day, and they're gloating now that it's here. That's a hard thing to hear from enemies.
